name: Assembly of Oaths
description:
Mechination makes bodies out of nothing: every part searches the next one by category, so the chain never runs the same way twice. Sacrilegion eats those bodies — its Sacraments demand monsters from BOTH sides of the field, which means the summon itself is the removal.

The trick is that your material is worthless on purpose. Oathling summons itself for free, Pledgebearer comes back from the Graveyard, and Kilnwarden reprints Level 1s every turn. You never feed anything you'd miss.

Slowest first turn in the set — there is nothing in your Graveyard to recycle yet. Survive two turns and the engine never stops.

name: The Quiet Hand
blurb: Play on their turn, not yours.
description:
This deck barely does anything in your own turn — and that is the point. Sleightwind monsters are discarded from your HAND during your opponent's turn to stop an attack, negate an effect, or bounce a monster. They never need to reach the field at all.

Manacle works the other half: mana that is taken during your opponent's turn is gone, because they already drew their fill. The Coupled effects let you choose — take a little now, or cut their NEXT turn short before it starts.

Choir of Two buys the discarded cards back, so you lose about half a card per round instead of a whole one. Meanwhile they keep not doing what they planned.

name: Kindle and Ash
blurb: Many small things, then one very large one.
description:
Six Level 1 beasts that pull each other onto the field for free. None of them is strong alone — the value is the count, and the count is also what your Reliquaries ask for.

Gravemaw turns the losses into fuel: everything that dies feeds the Graveyard, and Kindlekin reads the Graveyard as a second hand.

The payoff is Kindlekin, the Last Ember: four monsters on the field, six cards in the Graveyard, four Mana and two banished — and then it destroys every monster on the table except BEAST. Your whole swarm survives. Theirs does not, unless they happen to play Beasts too.

name: Tide and Tempest
blurb: Give it back, take it again.
description:
Water that returns and wind that never lands. Tidebound pulls cards back to hands and decks — including yours, on purpose — so the same good card gets played over and over.

Fethaerbreese fills the gaps: cheap fliers that summon themselves while a "Fethaerbreese" monster is already out, and spells that make attacking into you a bad idea.

The friendliest of the five to learn on. Nothing here demands a long setup, there is no hard combo to memorise, and a bad opening hand still plays out. If you have never played a card game like this, start here.

name: Forge and Fang
description:
The straightforward one. Wyldpack swarms and grows — the more wolves you control, the harder each of them hits. Forgeheart hands out Artifacts that stay equipped, so a Level 1 body ends up swinging like a Level 3.

There is almost no recursion and no denial. You put monsters down, you make them bigger, you attack. When it works it ends games two turns before anyone else's deck gets going.

The weakness is honest: if your board gets wiped you have no engine to rebuild from. Trade early, keep a card in reserve, and do not overextend into a full opposing field.
